summary.en: Bob Dylan begins adding electric instruments to his music—a marker for the birth of folk rock.
summary.zh: Bob Dylan开始在音乐中加入电声乐器，标志着folk rock的诞生。

body.zh:
Bob Dylan开始在音乐中加入电声乐器，标志着folk rock的诞生。

上节课我们强调了Bob Dylan先以传统民谣歌手的身份出现，到1965年早期音乐生涯的转变，他从一个传统的民谣歌手转变为了singer-songwriter（歌手创作人）。现在我们来讲讲美国回应的重要时刻，美国流行乐史60年代最重要的时刻之一，就是Bob Dylan开始在音乐中加入电声乐器。

为什么Bob Dylan使用电吉他是件有争议的事情呢？难道不是所有的摇滚乐手都使用电吉他吗？在民谣运动中，电吉他如果应用在传统的电声布鲁斯比如Chess Blues，是完全没问题的，是极好的。但是对于主要身份是民谣歌手的人而言，对于更关注于歌词的音乐，如果在其中应用电吉他，就会听起来很商业化，很像调幅（AM）电台播出的那种新潮少男少女们偏爱的音乐。因此Bob Dylan在民谣音乐里加入电声的行为，是一种对把他视为英雄的民谣传统主义者的背叛，像打脸一样。有趣的是，如果你回头看看Bob Dylan的历史，第一次用电吉他震惊世人的专辑是1965年3月的《Bringing It All Back Home》。但是在他之前的唱片中，不仅有些歌曲已经使用了电吉他，在一些未被收录的歌曲中，他也用电吉他尝试了rockabilly风格的音乐。因此在他看来这并非一个特别大的转变。何况在转变为民谣风格之前，他也很喜欢rock and roll。但是无论如何，Bob Dylan使用电声乐器还是引起了巨大反响。其实专辑并没有完全电声化，《Bringing It All Back Home》中一半是原声乐器，另一半是电声。主打歌《Subterranean Homesick Blues》以单曲形式发行，并在1965年夏季位列榜单39名。这种混合了电吉他和民谣的风格被称为民谣摇滚（folk rock），或者我们可以称之为美国民谣摇滚。这首《Subterranean Homesick Blues》标志了这种风格的诞生，Bob Dylan成为了风格创立者。

然而当Bob Dylan在Newport Folk音乐节出现时还是引发了麻烦，传统民谣音乐人都会在这个盛大的年度节日上演出，当Dylan带着一支乐队上台的时候，他获得了满场嘘声，甚至有人对他尖叫，他们觉得这个人背叛了他们。关于Pete Seeger（美国民谣音乐人）在现场的表现有很多传说，当然大部分都不准确：有人说他捂着耳朵满场跑；也有人说他跑到后台的车里摇上车窗，就听不到Dylan了；更有甚者说他到处跑着去拔扩音器的电源，把电源插头从墙上拽下来。不管你信哪个版本，也不管当时到底什么情况，有一点可以确定，那就是Pete Seeger很不喜欢Bob Dylan的音乐。也有人说人们大喊大叫并不是因为不喜欢电吉他，而是因为它声音太大导致他们听不清。我也不清楚实情，但是历史记载就是Bob Dylan被从Newport Folk音乐节上驱逐，主要因为他弹了电吉他。被驱逐这件事导致他对传统民谣势力愈发不满，他也基本上断绝了和他们的关系。那个夏天他发行了代表作，就是位列榜单第二，差不多与Newport Folk音乐节同时发行的《Like a Rolling Stone》。 这首歌既是他的一首热门歌曲，也是他转变风格后的第二首上榜歌曲。带着愤怒的情绪，Bob Dylan在1965年9月发行了歌曲《Positively Fourth Street》，通篇歌曲一段段地指向传统民谣势力，称他们不过是虚伪的朋友，以为他们在乎他，而他们不过只在乎自己而已。很大程度上这首歌意味着他与传统民谣的正式决裂。

这种加入电声的Dylan式音乐，有什么有趣和特殊的地方呢？实际上这种音乐的根本组成部分是电吉他、鼓和贝斯伴奏下的民谣音乐，或者至少称之为唱singer-songwriter类型的音乐。这种声音很美国化，确实受到了The Beatles的影响，但是与The Beatles的做法不完全相同。这些唱片有趣的地方是Al Kooper的风琴（organ）演奏。Al Kooper是摇滚史上的一个传奇人物，他写过歌也当过制作人，大部分时间在幕后，做过很多方面的工作。顺便说下，Al Kooper的名字是K开头的，和以后讲到70年Theatrical Rock（戏剧摇滚）时要说的Alice Cooper不同。在Bob Dylan录制《Bringing it All Back Home》的时候，Al Kooper希望作为一个吉他手加入。但他们已经有一个吉他手，叫Michael Bloomfield，是纽约地区很有名的电声布鲁斯吉他手。于是Al Kooper就走到风琴前面，他并不怎么弹风琴，但是弹一些和弦还是可以的。他们听《Like a Rolling Stone》的录音回放时，Bob Dylan说把风琴的声音调大点，制作人Tom Wilson说还是别听风琴了，那人不怎么会弹。Dylan说，不，我想听那风琴。Kooper这种近乎业余的哈蒙风琴（Hammond Organ）演奏，构成了Bob Dylan那个时期音乐中最重要的部分之一。听《Like A Rolling Stone》和《Positively 4th Street》时，重点听听Al Kooper的风琴与Bob Dylan的嗓音一起传达的效果，就可以体会到这种风格是怎么构成的了。Kooper常会讲他和Dylan巡演的故事。他们每到一个地方，都会去唱片店买唱片带回宾馆听。他们一张接一张地听，发现随着Dylan音乐的流行，人们开始模仿Al Kooper的风琴演奏。Al Kooper觉得，有人模仿这种风格，简直是世界上最好笑的事。

Dylan在65年到66年依然持续着超高人气，重要的是不仅加入电声乐器，他也成为一位重要的表演者。直到1965年中期之前，就算他不只是个歌曲创作者（songwriter），但他也从未真正被看做是表演者（performer）。1965年，他才成为我们熟知的那个Bob Dylan，完全靠自己成为了一个明星，不仅是一位歌曲创作者，也是一位表演者。

在那之后，《Highway 61 Revisited》于1965年8月发行，《Blonde on Blonde》于1966年夏天发行。但之后Dylan在纽约州北部伍德斯托克市郊发生了摩托车车祸，没人准确知道他伤势如何。这场事故和修养期间，他暂时离开了音乐产业。后来提及这段事，他说自己是故意的。可能由于周围的世界对他而言变化太快了吧，名声和财富以及与之俱来的一切笼罩在他周围，让他困扰，因此他决定退出一段时间。64到66年关于Dylan的故事值得我们思考，因为到他60年代末复出的时候，情况已大有不同，我们不再考虑美国对英伦入侵的回应了。

如果把Dylan视为60年代美国回应的中心人物之一，我们应该考虑下除他之外还有什么重要人物，以及Dylan对他们有什么影响，这就是我们下节课要讲的内容。
body.en:
Bob Dylan begins adding electric instruments to his music—a marker for the birth of folk rock.

Last time we stressed Dylan’s path from traditional folk singer to singer-songwriter by early 1965. Now a key moment in America’s reply—and one of the most important in 1960s U.S. pop: Dylan goes electric.

Why is Dylan on electric guitar controversial? Don’t all rock players use electric guitars? In the folk world, electric guitar is fine in traditional electric blues such as Chess blues—excellent, even. But for someone cast mainly as a folk singer, for lyric-first music, electric guitar can sound commercial, like the AM-radio teen fare. So adding electric sound to folk reads as betrayal to folk traditionalists who treat him as a hero—a slap in the face. Interestingly, if you look back, the album that shocks with electric guitar is March 1965’s Bringing It All Back Home. Yet earlier records already have some electric tracks, and unreleased cuts try rockabilly with electric guitar. To him it is not a huge leap—and before folk he already liked rock and roll. Still, going electric causes a huge reaction. The LP is not fully electric: half acoustic, half electric. Lead track “Subterranean Homesick Blues” is issued as a single and reaches No. 39 in summer 1965. This mix of electric guitar and folk is called folk rock—or American folk rock. “Subterranean Homesick Blues” marks the style’s birth; Dylan is its founder.

Trouble still hits when he appears at the Newport Folk Festival, the big annual gathering for traditional folk. Dylan walks on with a band and gets booed; some scream that he has betrayed them. Many legends surround Pete Seeger that night—mostly inaccurate: covering his ears and running; shutting himself in a car so he cannot hear; yanking amp plugs from the wall. Whatever version you believe, Seeger dislikes Dylan’s music that night. Some say the shouting is not hatred of electric guitar but volume that buries the words. I do not know the full truth; the historical story is that Dylan is driven off Newport mainly for playing electric guitar. That expulsion hardens him against traditional folk power; he largely cuts ties. That summer he issues his signature hit—almost concurrent with Newport—“Like a Rolling Stone,” which peaks at No. 2, his second chart single after the style shift. Angry, he releases “Positively 4th Street” in September 1965, aimed stanza by stanza at traditional folk circles as false friends who care only for themselves. In large part it is a formal break with traditional folk.

What is interesting and special about this electric Dylan sound? At base it is folk—or at least singer-songwriter singing—backed by electric guitar, drums, and bass. It sounds American, Beatles-influenced but not identical to the Beatles’ method. A striking part of these records is Al Kooper’s organ. Kooper is a rock-history figure—writer, producer, mostly behind the scenes. Note: Kooper starts with K; not Alice Cooper of later theatrical rock. During Bringing It All Back Home sessions Kooper wants in as a guitarist, but they already have Michael Bloomfield, a noted New York electric-blues player. So Kooper sits at the organ—he is not really an organist, but he can play chords. On playback of “Like a Rolling Stone,” Dylan asks to turn the organ up; producer Tom Wilson says forget it, the guy cannot play. Dylan insists. Kooper’s near-amateur Hammond becomes one of the period’s defining parts. On “Like a Rolling Stone” and “Positively 4th Street,” listen to Kooper’s organ with Dylan’s voice to hear how the style is built. Kooper often tells tour stories: in each town they buy records and listen in hotel rooms; as Dylan’s music spreads, people start copying Kooper’s organ. To him, being imitated is the funniest thing in the world.

Through 1965–66 Dylan stays hugely popular—and not only electric: he becomes an important performer. Before mid-1965, even when he is more than a songwriter, he is not really cast as a star performer. In 1965 he becomes the Bob Dylan we know—a star on his own, writer and performer.

Then Highway 61 Revisited (August 1965) and Blonde on Blonde (summer 1966). After that, a motorcycle crash near Woodstock in upstate New York; no one knows the injuries exactly. Through accident and recovery he steps away from the industry for a while. Later he says it was deliberate—maybe the world around him moved too fast; fame, money, and everything that came with them pressed in, so he pulled back. The 1964–66 Dylan story matters because by his late-1960s return the frame has changed; we are no longer talking America’s reply to the Invasion.

If Dylan is one center of that 1960s reply, we should ask who else matters and how Dylan shapes them—that is next.
